questions.question: A patient presents with parotitis that appears consistent with mumps.
questions.question_raw: A patient presents with parotitis. Appears consistent with mumps.

parts.text: What is the most common cause of bacterial (suppurative) parotitis?
Give two modalities for diagnosing mumps.
What are three complications of mumps?

parts_raw.text: What is the most common cause of bacterial parotitis?

questions.model_answer:
a) Staphylococcus aureus (suppurative parotitis; gram-negative organisms are the other main cause), typically in postoperative, premature, or debilitated patients with poor oral intake.
b) (1) RT-PCR of a buccal/oral (Stensen duct) swab, saliva, urine or CSF. (2) Serology showing mumps IgM (by ELISA) or a fourfold rise in acute/convalescent titres; viral isolation/culture is a further option.
c) (1) Epididymo-orchitis/oophoritis. (2) Aseptic meningitis (and rarely encephalitis). (3) Transient high-frequency deafness. (Others: pancreatitis, arthritis, myocarditis, oophoritis.)

cohort_answer.text: Staph aureus. || Buccal PCR, IgM. || AOM; Aseptic meningitis; Orchitis/oophoritis; Deafness.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy presents with a 3-day history of bilateral testicular pain after returning from a school trip to Eastern Europe. He had a preceding febrile illness with fever and malaise about 3 weeks into his trip. On examination he has swelling and tenderness of both testes and epididymides, with some submandibular swelling but no swollen glands. This picture is consistent with mumps epididymo-orchitis.
questions.question_raw: You see a 15 year-old boy presenting with a 3-day history of bilateral testicular pain. He recently returned from a school trip to East Europe. He had a preceding febrile illness with fever and malaise approximately 3 weeks into his trip. On examination, he has swelling and tenderness of both testes and epididymides. He has some submandibular swelling but no swollen glands.

parts.text: List two tests that should be performed to make the diagnosis.

parts_raw.text: List TWO tests that should be performed to make the diagnosis.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Mumps RT-PCR on a buccal/oral swab (or urine/serum). (2) Mumps IgM serology by ELISA (with a convalescent titre if the initial IgM is negative). These confirm mumps as the cause of the epididymo-orchitis.

questions.question: A young girl presents with symptoms of mumps.
questions.question_raw:
Q42 (2011 AM, 2011 PM, 2008)
Young girl with symptoms of Mumps
questions.model_answer:
a) Manifestations: incubation 16-18 days; nonspecific prodrome (low-grade fever, anorexia, malaise, headache), then earache and tender parotid enlargement over 2-3 days (unilateral in ~25%), obscuring the angle of the mandible and lifting the ear lobe; edematous/erythematous Stensen duct orifice; submandibular/sublingual sialadenitis in ~10%; many infections subclinical.
b) DDX of parotitis: (1) Other viral parotitis - parainfluenza 3, coxsackievirus, influenza A, EBV, HHV-6, HIV. (2) Suppurative bacterial parotitis (S. aureus, gram-negatives) - warm, hard, tender gland with purulent Stensen duct drainage. (3) Noninfectious - drugs (phenylbutazone, thiouracil, iodides, phenothiazines), metabolic (diabetes, malnutrition, cirrhosis, uremia), tumours/cysts/stones, Sjogren, sarcoid (uveoparotid fever), Mikulicz/Parinaud syndromes.
c) Diagnostic tests: confirmation unnecessary in typical cases; otherwise RT-PCR (buccal/oral swab, saliva, urine, CSF; more sensitive than culture), IgM serology by ELISA or fourfold rise between acute/convalescent sera, and viral isolation. Elevated serum amylase supports salivary involvement; ELISA is used to assess immunity.
d) Complications: (1) Epididymo-orchitis (20-30% of postpubertal men, bilateral in 1/6). (2) Oophoritis (5% of postpubertal women). (3) Aseptic meningitis (1-10%) and encephalitis (~0.1%). (4) Transient high-frequency deafness (~4%). (Others: pancreatitis, arthritis, myocarditis/ECG changes, mild renal dysfunction.)
e) Vaccination in outbreaks: a two-dose MMR regimen is recommended for those without evidence of immunity; ACIP (2018) recommends a third dose of MMR for persons at increased risk during an outbreak. Post-exposure immunization may not protect against the current natural infection but protects against future exposure.
f) Family: Paramyxoviridae (genus Orthorubulavirus/Rubulavirus).
questions.beyond_mandell: The genus/family classification (Paramyxoviridae; Rubulavirus/Orthorubulavirus) is standard ICTV taxonomy; the read slice references the paramyxovirus/MMR context but does not state the taxonomic name explicitly.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Incubation period: 16-18 days (range 12-25). Most Infectious: 2 days before, 5 days after parotitis onset (virus isolated from saliva 7d prior and 9 days after). Symptoms: many subclinical; may have a few days fever, myalgia, malaise, followed by nonsuppurative parotitis within 48h. Complications: orchitis/oophoritis, meningitis/encephalitis, deafness. Self-limited, takes a few weeks to fully recover

B: For parotitis - Bacterial: S aureus, Gram negative organisms (often unilateral swollen gland with overlying erythema, purulent drainage from Stenson's duct with parotid massage, post-op/debilitated patients with poor oral intake, premature infants). Viral: Influenza A, Coxsackie, Parainfluenza (adenovirus, EBV, CMV, LCMV, HSV, HIV) - prodromal phase. Noninfectious: Drugs (bilateral, asymptomatic - Phenylbutazone, thiouracil, iodides); Other: diabetes, malnutrition, cirrhosis, uremia, Sjogrens, tumour, parotid stone

C: RT-PCR: buccal/oral swab, serum, urine, CSF. PHOL: do both urine and buccal. Can also send for culture. Serology: positive IgM - may not be positive until 5 days after onset of symptoms, remains positive for 4 weeks, repeat IgM in 5-10 days if negative. Serologic tests cannot differentiate between vaccination and prior mumps exposure, and the level of mumps IgG antibody needed for protection is not known

D: Orchitis/Oophoritis (5-10d after onset of parotitis), Aseptic meningitis, Encephalitis, Deafness (acute onset), Myocarditis, Thyroiditis, Pancreatitis, Interstitial nephritis, Arthritis

E: Mumps vaccination and IG in non-immune exposed individuals does not alter course of disease if it develops. However, recommend vaccination of susceptible individuals as this will protect against future exposures. Born after 1970 and received <2 doses of MMR (age varies by province), no laboratory-confirmed mumps, no documented immunity. Efficacy of vaccine: 60-90% with 1 dose, 75-95% with 2 doses; immunity wanes over time. NB: Mumps occurs even in fully vaccinated adults, although vaccination limits size, duration, and spread of outbreaks.

F: Family: Paramyxoviridae, Genus: Rubulavirus, Species: Mumps rubulavirus

For each virus, name one antiviral with activity against it, if any (Mumps is given as an example). Viruses: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), Influenza, Zika, Ebola.
questions.question_raw: In the following table, fill out if the virus is RNA/DNA, and whether it is enveloped or not. For each virus, name one antiviral that has activity against it, if any (Mumps is given as an example). Table columns: Virus, RNA or DNA, Enveloped (Yes or No), Antiviral. Viruses listed: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Influenza, Zika, Ebola.

parts.text: Complete the table (RNA/DNA, enveloped Yes/No, one antiviral) for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, Epstein-Barr virus, Influenza, Zika, Ebola.

parts_raw.text: Fill out the table for RNA/DNA, enveloped status, and antiviral for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Influenza, Zika, Ebola

questions.model_answer:
a) Virus | RNA/DNA | Enveloped | Antiviral
(1) Mumps (example) | RNA | Yes | None (supportive care only)
(2) Measles | RNA | Yes | None approved (ribavirin used off-label in severe/immunocompromised cases)
(3) Hepatitis B | DNA | Yes | Tenofovir or entecavir (nucleos[t]ide analogue); pegylated interferon is an alternative
(4) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) | DNA | Yes | None of proven clinical benefit (acyclovir/ganciclovir have in vitro activity but do not alter disease)
(5) Influenza | RNA | Yes | Oseltamivir (neuraminidase inhibitor); baloxavir (endonuclease inhibitor) is an alternative
(6) Zika | RNA | Yes | None (no licensed antiviral; supportive care)
(7) Ebola | RNA | Yes | Monoclonal antibodies (atoltivimab/maftivimab/odesivimab [Inmazeb] or ansuvimab [Ebanga]); remdesivir/favipiravir investigational
questions.beyond_mandell: Virus taxonomy/RNA-vs-DNA and envelope status, and the HBV, measles, EBV, Zika and Ebola monoclonal-antibody specifics are standard virology/Mandell species chapters plus FDA/WHO Ebola guidance, not this General Principles chapter.

questions.model_answer:
Mumps: RNA; enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive).
Measles: RNA; enveloped; no specific antiviral (vitamin A adjunct; ribavirin unproven).
Hepatitis B: DNA; enveloped; yes - nucleos(t)ide analogues (tenofovir, entecavir), peginterferon.
EBV: DNA; enveloped; no established antiviral (aciclovir/ganciclovir have limited activity).
Ebola: RNA; enveloped; yes - monoclonal antibodies (atoltivimab-maftivimab-odesivimab [Inmazeb], ansuvimab [Ebanga]).
Zika: RNA; enveloped; none.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only measles (RNA, enveloped, ribavirin unproven, Mandell p. 2116) is covered by this chapter; the other rows are from general virology and current IDSA/CDC therapeutics.
